title: Halimah's thin donkey
hookLine: the sirah tells how Halimah's donkey and flock grew strong once she took the baby home

cards: A donkey so weak it keeps falling behind the others. A she-camel with no milk. A baby crying all night because his mother has nothing to give him.
That is how Halimah, a woman of the Banu Sa'd, arrives in Mecca, the sirah says, in a year of drought.

She and the other women of her tribe have come to find babies to nurse, because Meccan families sent their infants out to the desert, and the fathers paid. And there's one baby nobody wants. Today: barakah.

teach.b: The baby is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and his father is dead. In Ibn Ishaq's telling, Halimah says every woman was offered him and turned him down, because an orphan's family couldn't be expected to pay much.
Every other woman finds a nursling. Halimah doesn't.

She doesn't want to be the only one riding home with empty arms, so she tells her husband she will go back and take the orphan. He answers, the sirah says, that perhaps God will bless them through him.
Then the story turns. As soon as she holds the boy, she has milk enough for him and for her own son, and both sleep.

teach.h: MILK, A FULL CAMEL, A FAST DONKEY.
teach.b: Her husband goes out to the old she-camel and finds her full. On the road home, the thin donkey that lagged on the way in now outpaces the whole caravan, and the other women call out: isn't this the same animal?

Back in the dry hills of Banu Sa'd, her sheep come home full of milk while the neighbors' flocks come back hungry, until the neighbors tell their shepherds to graze wherever Halimah's shepherd grazes.
The Arabic word for what fills this story is barakah: blessing, increase, good that stays. Notice where it begins.

Not with a reward for a clever choice, but with a woman taking the child nobody else took, almost out of embarrassment. These stories come from the sirah, not the Qur'an, and later writers told them warmly.
But the Qur'an itself remembers the orphan.

teach.h: DID HE NOT FIND THEE AN ORPHAN AND PROTECT (THEE)?
teach.b: In surah ninety-three, Pickthall translates: "Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?"

how: Halimah is remembered by Muslims as the Prophet's ﷺ foster mother, and the sirah's account of her journey is often retold when speaking of barakah and of care for orphans.

o: a reward earned by making a clever choice
blessing: good that comes, stays and grows
the milk a nursing mother gives a baby

games.q: Halimah's thin donkey — tap the pairs.
p: a woman of the Banu Sa'd
lagged in, then led the way home

s: the women all competed to nurse the Prophet
in the sirah, every woman turned him down because he was an orphan.
Halimah's husband said God might bless them through the boy
so the sirah tells it, before the blessing came.
the story of the donkey is told in the Qur'an
it comes from the sirah; the Qur'an remembers him as an orphan God protected.

games.q: you're Halimah. every other woman has a baby to nurse. the only one left is an orphan whose family can't pay much. what do you do?
o: go back and take the orphan.
wait in Mecca for another family.
games.why: she took him, the sirah says, so as not to go home empty-handed, and the blessing came after.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose arrival made your life fuller in a way you didn't plan: a child, a neighbor, a friend who came in through a side door, someone you took on because no one else would.
Let their face come clearly, and notice what grew after they came. If you pray, you can thank Allah for them by name; if you don't, just stay with the fullness and the face.

wordCard.voice: Barakah: blessing, increase, good that stays, the word the sirah uses for what filled Halimah's story when she took the baby nobody wanted. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: barakah, blessing, the good that comes and stays.

carryVoice: Your line: blessing came with him. Tomorrow, the opening of the chest. Day seven hundred seven.
